practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a characteristic of good mental health according to the specification?
A) An absence of all emotions
B) Positive engagement with society
C) Complete freedom from stress
D) A diagnosis of no mental illness
practice_questions.marks: B) Positive engagement with society [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'mental health'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A definition that states psychological wellbeing AND that a person can cope with normal stresses and function effectively in daily life or society — both elements clearly expressed.
Secure: Both elements present but one expressed vaguely.
Developing: Mentions either coping or wellbeing but not both.
Emerging: Vague or incorrect definition.

practice_questions.text: Describe two reasons why the reported incidence of significant mental health problems has changed over time.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks. Students may include: increased challenges of modern living (e.g. isolation, financial pressure) leading to more actual cases; increased recognition of the nature of mental health problems meaning people identify and report symptoms more readily; lessening of social stigma meaning more people are willing to disclose difficulties and seek help.
Mastering: Two distinct reasons, each developed with an explanation of how it leads to higher reported rates.
Secure: Two reasons correctly identified with brief development.
Developing: One reason with development, or two without.
Emerging: One reason named without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which a significant mental health problem can affect an individual's daily life.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct individual effects (e.g. damage to relationships AND difficulties coping with daily life or negative impact on physical wellbeing), each explained with how/why the mental health problem causes that effect. Two developed points.
Secure: Two effects identified with some explanation of the link.
Developing: Two effects named without explanation, or one developed effect.
Emerging: One vague effect mentioned.

practice_questions.text: Describe the ways in which significant mental health problems can affect both individuals and society.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for covering: individual effects — damage to relationships (1); difficulties coping with day-to-day life (1); negative impact on physical wellbeing (1); societal effects — need for more social care (1); increased crime rates or implications for the economy (1).
Mastering: At least three individual effects and two societal effects, each described clearly.
Secure: Two from each category.
Developing: Three effects total, both individual and societal mentioned.
Emerging: Only individual or only societal, or effects are vague.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the idea that reporting rates of mental health problems in the UK have increased over time.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Describes at least two of the three reasons (isolation/modern challenges, recognition, reduced stigma) with elaboration; evaluates by considering whether the increase reflects real higher rates or better reporting (methodological issue), considers the role of changing diagnostic criteria, and discusses implications; each evaluation point developed with a reason.
Secure: Two reasons described; two evaluative points with some development.
Developing: One reason described; one evaluative point.
Emerging: Vague reference to more people having mental health problems; evaluation absent or a single unsupported sentence.
[AO1 ~4 marks; AO3 ~5 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of procedural memory?
A) Remembering what you ate for lunch yesterday
B) Knowing that London is the capital of England
C) Being able to ride a bike without thinking about it
D) Recalling your first day at primary school
practice_questions.marks: C) Being able to ride a bike without thinking about it [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'encoding' in the context of memory.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Precise definition stating that encoding is the process of converting information into a form that can be stored in the memory system, with accurate psychological language.
Secure: Clear definition capturing the input/conversion aspect of encoding.
Developing: Partial definition — may describe what happens but lacks precision about the conversion process.
Emerging: Vague attempt, such as 'when you remember something.'

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between episodic memory and semantic memory.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear, developed distinction — episodic is memory for personally experienced events tied to a specific time and place (e.g. recalling a holiday); semantic is memory for general knowledge and facts not linked to personal experience (e.g. knowing the capital of France); difference is clearly stated and illustrated.
Secure: Both types described accurately with the key distinction evident.
Developing: One type described correctly; the other is vague or only partially accurate.
Emerging: Names the types without meaningful description.

practice_questions.text: Ravi is learning to play the guitar. After months of practice, he can play a chord sequence automatically without looking at his hands. Explain what type of memory Ravi is using and why.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies procedural memory and provides a developed explanation — procedural memory stores how to perform learned skills and operates automatically without conscious thought; links directly to the scenario (playing chords without conscious attention).
Secure: Correct identification of procedural memory with a clear explanation referencing the scenario.
Developing: Correct identification but explanation is limited or does not engage with the scenario.
Emerging: Names a type of memory without explanation or engagement with the scenario.

practice_questions.text: Describe the three types of long-term memory.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: All three types (episodic, semantic, procedural) described accurately with a clear distinguishing feature and a relevant example for each; responses are precise and use correct terminology throughout.
Secure: All three types described correctly; descriptions are accurate but may lack a developed example for one type.
Developing: Two types described correctly; the third is missing or inaccurate.
Emerging: One type described, or descriptions are too vague to distinguish between the types.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the three processes of memory: encoding, storage and retrieval.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (AO1): Encoding converts information into a storable form; storage holds the information; retrieval brings it back into awareness. All three are required for a memory to be usable. Types of encoding include visual, acoustic and semantic; deeper encoding tends to produce stronger memories.
Evaluation (AO3): The model is useful because it distinguishes three separable stages, which helps explain different types of memory failure (e.g. encoding failure vs retrieval failure). However, the model is simplified — in reality the stages interact rather than operating as a neat sequence. The concept of retrieval failure is well supported (e.g. the tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon) but encoding quality is difficult to measure directly, reducing scientific precision.
Mastering: Accurate, detailed description of all three processes plus at least two developed evaluation points with elaboration.
Secure: All three processes described and two evaluation points made, though elaboration may be limited on one.
Developing: At least two processes described and one evaluation point made.
Emerging: Brief or inaccurate description; evaluation absent or only a single undeveloped point.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes conformity?
A) Obeying a direct order from an authority figure
B) Changing behaviour or belief due to real or imagined group pressure
C) Helping a stranger in an emergency situation
D) Being influenced by an expert in a field
practice_questions.marks: B) Changing behaviour or belief due to real or imagined group pressure [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'anonymity' in the context of conformity research.
practice_questions.marks: Anonymity is the condition of not being personally identified or observed by the group [1 mark], which reduces the social pressure to conform because the individual does not fear public judgement or rejection [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Describe one social factor and one dispositional factor that affect conformity to majority influence.
practice_questions.marks:
Social factor: e.g. group size — as the number of people in the majority increases, the social pressure on the individual to conform also increases [1 mark], though the effect levels off beyond a certain group size [1 mark].
Disposition factor: e.g. expertise — a person with specialist knowledge in the topic is less likely to conform because they trust their own informed judgement rather than the group’s view [1 mark].
[Accept any accurate social factor + dispositional factor with development; 2 marks for the social factor, 1 for the dispositional factor, or 1+2 respectively.]

practice_questions.text: A student is asked to estimate the length of a line in a group activity. She can clearly see the correct answer but the rest of the group all say a different length out loud. Using your knowledge of conformity, explain why she might go along with the group.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies and explains two factors clearly linked to the scenario with psychological terminology (e.g. public setting increases social pressure because the student’s response is visible to others; majority group creates pressure to conform to avoid standing out).
Secure: Identifies and explains one factor clearly linked to the scenario.
Developing: Names a relevant factor (e.g. group pressure) but does not link it specifically to the scenario details.
Emerging: Makes a vague reference to fitting in or peer pressure without psychological framing.

practice_questions.text: Describe Asch's study of conformity.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate aim, method (confederates, line-matching task, 12 critical trials), results (approx. 37% conformity on critical trials, 75% conformed at least once, conformity fell with private responses), and conclusion (people conform to majority even when clearly wrong) — all four elements present and precise.
Secure: Three of the four elements (aim, method, results, conclusion) described accurately with relevant detail.
Developing: Two elements present or one element described in good detail; some inaccuracy.
Emerging: A vague account of the study with limited or no specific details about the procedure or findings.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the factors that affect conformity to majority influence.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate and detailed description of social factors (group size, anonymity, task difficulty) AND dispositional factors (personality, expertise) with psychological terminology; evaluation includes at least two developed points (e.g. Asch’s findings support the role of anonymity because conformity fell with private responses; however, the sample lacked diversity, limiting generalisability) with elaboration.
Secure: Description covers most factors with reasonable accuracy; evaluation includes two points with some development.
Developing: Description of two or three factors with some accuracy; evaluation present but limited or repetitive.
Emerging: Brief, underdeveloped description of one or two factors; evaluation is a single sentence without elaboration.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a binocular depth cue?
A) Linear perspective
B) Retinal disparity
C) Height in plane
D) Occlusion
practice_questions.marks: B) Retinal disparity [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'perception'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Precise definition stating that perception is the brain’s active process of interpreting and giving meaning to the raw sensory information received from the senses.
Secure: Clear definition capturing the interpretive, meaningful aspect of perception.
Developing: Partial definition — describes seeing or experiencing without capturing the interpretive, brain-based process.
Emerging: Confuses perception with sensation, e.g. ‘when your eyes detect light.’

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by 'occlusion' as a monocular depth cue.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Defines occlusion as when one object partially blocks another from view; explains that the blocked object is perceived as further away; developed with a clear example (e.g. a lamp post blocking part of a building in the distance).
Secure: Defines occlusion and explains the depth perception consequence.
Developing: Describes blocking but does not explain the depth perception implication.
Emerging: Vague response or confusion with another depth cue.

practice_questions.text: Priya is looking at a railway line stretching into the distance. The tracks appear to get closer together as they recede. Explain which depth cue Priya is using and why it helps her judge distance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies linear perspective; explains that parallel lines appear to converge at a vanishing point as distance increases; links clearly to the scenario (the tracks appearing to come together) and explains that the degree of convergence provides depth information.
Secure: Correct identification with clear explanation engaging the scenario.
Developing: Correct identification but explanation is limited or does not clearly reference the scenario.
Emerging: Names a depth cue without explanation or scenario engagement.

practice_questions.text: Describe the two binocular depth cues.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Retinal disparity defined as the difference between left and right eye images, with explanation that closer objects produce greater disparity and the brain calculates depth from this; convergence defined as the inward turning of both eyes to focus on close objects, with explanation that greater muscular effort signals closer objects; both described with accurate terminology.
Secure: Both cues described accurately; one may lack a fully developed explanation.
Developing: Both named with partial descriptions; one may be inaccurate.
Emerging: Only one cue described or both very vague.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the role of depth cues in visual perception.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (AO1): Four monocular cues (height in plane, relative size, occlusion, linear perspective) and two binocular cues (retinal disparity, convergence); each described with how it provides depth information; distinction between monocular and binocular.
Evaluation (AO3): Strength — depth cues are supported by consistent everyday observations and demonstrate the sophistication of the visual system. Strength — knowledge of depth cues has practical applications in art, film and virtual reality design. Weakness — monocular depth cues work in 2D images as well as real 3D scenes, suggesting the brain uses inference from experience rather than purely bottom-up information (supporting Gregory over Gibson). Weakness — individual differences exist; people with certain conditions (e.g. amblyopia) may not process binocular cues effectively.
Mastering: Accurate description with at least two developed evaluation points.
Secure: Depth cues described and two evaluation points made.
Developing: Some cues described; one evaluation point.
Emerging: Brief or partial description; evaluation absent or undeveloped.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes Piaget's view on the relationship between language and thought?
A) Language and thought develop at the same time with neither depending on the other
B) Language shapes and determines how we think about the world
C) Language depends on thought — cognitive development comes first
D) Thought is impossible without language
practice_questions.marks: C) Language depends on thought — cognitive development comes first [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis.
practice_questions.marks: The Sapir-Whorf hypothesis proposes that the language a person speaks shapes or determines how they think and perceive the world [1 mark], so people who speak different languages may think about or perceive the world differently [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Describe one piece of evidence that supports the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis.
practice_questions.marks: Evidence from colour recognition: different languages divide the colour spectrum into different categories [1 mark]. Research has shown that speakers of languages with more distinct colour terms can more easily distinguish and recognise shades in that region of the spectrum [1 mark]. This supports the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis because it suggests language categories influence perception [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Two psychologists are debating whether language shapes thought or whether thought comes before language. Psychologist A cites evidence that young children understand concepts before they can name them. Psychologist B cites evidence that colour terms in different languages affect colour recognition. Explain what each piece of evidence tells us about the relationship between language and thought.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Psychologist A's evidence supports Piaget — children possess cognitive concepts (e.g. object permanence) before having the words for them, showing thought precedes language; Psychologist B's evidence supports Sapir-Whorf — language categories (colour terms) influence a perceptual skill (colour recognition), showing language shapes thought. Both points explicitly linked to the scenario.
Secure: Both positions identified and linked to evidence; one explanation clearly developed.
Developing: Both positions identified but explanations vague or not linked to the scenario details.
Emerging: One position identified without development.

practice_questions.text: Describe Piaget's theory of the relationship between language and thought.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate description of Piaget's position (language depends on thought, not the other way around); clear explanation that cognitive development precedes language acquisition; concrete example of a concept developing before its label (e.g. object permanence, conservation); implications for how children learn; links to Piaget's stage theory of cognitive development.
Secure: Main position described accurately with some development and at least one example.
Developing: States Piaget's position but does not develop it or provide examples.
Emerging: Vague or partially inaccurate description.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the view that language shapes thought.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate description of Sapir-Whorf hypothesis (strong and weak versions); evidence from colour recognition and event recall; cross-cultural examples; evaluation includes at least two developed points (e.g. strong version rejected because people think thoughts for which they have no words; weak version supported by colour and spatial reasoning research; contrast with Piaget's view; interactive account as a synthesis).
Secure: Description of the hypothesis with evidence; evaluation of two points with some development.
Developing: Description of hypothesis; evaluation limited or underdeveloped.
Emerging: Brief description; minimal or single-sentence evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which part of the nervous system controls the fight or flight response?
A) The central nervous system
B) The somatic nervous system
C) The sympathetic autonomic nervous system
D) The parasympathetic autonomic nervous system
practice_questions.marks: C) The sympathetic autonomic nervous system [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'autonomic nervous system'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise definition stating it is the division of the PNS that controls involuntary bodily functions such as heart rate, digestion or breathing — both the involuntary nature and a specific function stated [2 marks].
Secure: Correct core idea — involuntary control — with vague or missing example [1 mark].
Developing: Partial answer identifying automatic processes without linking to the PNS [0–1 mark].
Emerging: Incorrect or irrelevant [0 marks].

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens to the body during the fight or flight response.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per accurate, distinct point up to 3 marks. Students may include: the sympathetic ANS is activated; adrenaline is released by the adrenal glands; heart rate increases; blood is redirected to the muscles; glucose is released for energy; digestion slows or stops; pupils dilate; breathing quickens.
Mastering: Three distinct, accurate physiological changes named with a brief explanation of why each occurs.
Secure: Three changes named with limited explanation.
Developing: Two changes named.
Emerging: One change named or vague description only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the James–Lange theory of emotion. In your answer, refer to the relationship between bodily changes and emotional experience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear statement that bodily changes precede and cause emotions (not the other way around), with an accurate example (e.g. heart races → we interpret this as fear) and a link to the role of the brain interpreting physical feedback. Two developed points.
Secure: Correct direction of causation stated and an example given; some explanation of the theory's logic.
Developing: Partially correct — may state correct direction but without explanation; or reversal of direction.
Emerging: Vague mention of the theory without accurate content.

practice_questions.text: Describe the structure and function of the human nervous system, including its main divisions.
practice_questions.marks:
This question asks students to describe the nervous system rather than a named study. Award marks for: CNS described as brain + spinal cord (1); PNS described as all nerves outside the CNS (1); somatic nervous system identified as controlling voluntary movement and sensory input (1); autonomic nervous system identified as controlling involuntary functions (1); sympathetic and parasympathetic branches distinguished in terms of function (1).
Mastering: All five elements accurately described with clear function for each division.
Secure: Four elements described.
Developing: Two or three divisions named with basic functions.
Emerging: Only CNS/PNS named without function.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the James–Lange theory of emotion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate description of the theory (bodily changes → brain interpretation → emotion; not emotion → body); at least two specific physical examples; two elaborated evaluation points (e.g. similar bodily states for different emotions as a weakness; spinal cord injury research as a strength), with each evaluation point developed with a reason.
Secure: Accurate description of direction of causation; two evaluation points with some development.
Developing: Partially correct description; one evaluation point with reasoning, or two without.
Emerging: Some relevant content but description is vague or direction reversed; evaluation is a single unsupported point.
[Description AO1 ~4 marks; Evaluation AO3 ~5 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a correctly operationalised hypothesis?
A) People who sleep more will feel better
B) Students who get more sleep will have higher exam scores
C) Participants who sleep for 8 hours will score higher on a 20-item memory test than participants who sleep for 4 hours
D) Sleep affects memory
practice_questions.marks: C) Participants who sleep for 8 hours will score higher on a 20-item memory test than participants who sleep for 4 hours [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define what is meant by an 'extraneous variable'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'Any variable, other than the IV, that could affect the DV and therefore reduce the validity of the study.' — both elements present and clearly linked.
Secure: Core idea correct — names variable other than IV and mentions DV or validity.
Developing: Vague — mentions something affecting results without reference to IV or DV.
Emerging: Incorrect or incomplete definition.

practice_questions.text: Describe how a researcher could use stratified sampling to select participants for a study.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- Divide the target population into subgroups (strata) based on relevant characteristics (e.g. age, gender, year group).
- Calculate the proportion each subgroup represents in the full population.
- Randomly select participants from each subgroup in proportion to its size.
Mastering: All three steps described clearly.
Secure: Two steps with correct terminology.
Developing: General idea of subgroups without proportionality.
Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: A researcher wants to study whether background music affects reading comprehension. Write a suitable alternative (experimental) hypothesis for this study.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should:
- State a directional or non-directional prediction.
- Operationalise the IV (e.g. two conditions: music vs no music, or specific type of music vs silence).
- Operationalise the DV (e.g. score on a 10-question comprehension test based on a given passage).
- Example: 'Participants who read a passage with background music playing will score lower on a 10-question comprehension test than participants who read in silence.'
Mastering: Both IV conditions and DV clearly operationalised, directional or non-directional stated.
Secure: IV and DV present, one not fully operationalised.
Developing: IV or DV missing.
Emerging: Vague prediction only.

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between a null hypothesis and an alternative hypothesis.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should cover:
- Null hypothesis: predicts no significant difference or relationship between variables; any result is due to chance.
- Alternative hypothesis: predicts there will be a difference or relationship; what the researcher expects.
- Both require operationalisation (both conditions of IV and measurable DV).
- After statistical testing: if results are significant, the null hypothesis is rejected and the alternative is supported.
- Psychologists support or reject hypotheses based on evidence; they do not 'prove' them.
Mastering: All five elements clearly and accurately described.
Secure: Four elements present.
Developing: Null and alternative distinguished, one or two additional points.
Emerging: Basic distinction only.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the four main sampling methods used in psychological research.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (AO1):
- Random: every member of population has equal chance; uses lottery or random numbers.
- Opportunity: selects whoever is available and willing.
- Systematic: selects every nth person from a list.
- Stratified: divides population into subgroups, selects proportionally from each.

Evaluation (AO3):
- Random: strength — unbiased and representative if done correctly. Weakness — requires full list; non-response bias.
- Opportunity: strength — quick, cheap, easy. Weakness — biased towards available groups; not representative.
- Systematic: strength — avoids researcher bias, straightforward. Weakness — may have pattern bias if list is structured.
- Stratified: strength — most representative method; reflects population structure. Weakness — time-consuming; requires detailed knowledge of population.
- Overall: stratified produces the most representative sample but opportunity is most commonly used due to practicality.

Mastering: All four methods described correctly, with elaborated strengths and weaknesses.
Secure: Three methods described well with evaluation.
Developing: Two methods described, some evaluation.
Emerging: One or two methods, limited evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following brain structures develops first?
A) Cortex
B) Cerebellum
C) Brain stem
D) Thalamus
practice_questions.marks: C) Brain stem [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define what is meant by 'autonomic functions'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear definition identifying (1) processes that happen automatically/without conscious thought, AND (2) a correct example such as breathing, heartbeat or digestion — e.g. 'Body processes that operate without conscious control, such as breathing and heart rate.' [2 marks].
Secure: Correct core idea but vague or missing example [1 mark].
Developing: Partial reference to automatic processes but imprecise [0–1 mark].
Emerging: Incorrect or very vague [0 marks].

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of the thalamus in brain development.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- The thalamus acts as a relay station for sensory information.
- It routes signals from the senses (sight, hearing, touch, etc.) to the correct area of the cortex.
- It develops after the brain stem but before the cerebellum and cortex.
- Newborns can respond to sensory stimuli partly because the thalamus is functional at birth.
Mastering: All three elements (function, timing, implication) clearly stated.
Secure: Two elements, terminology correct.
Developing: One element with some accuracy.
Emerging: Limited or vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain how both nature and nurture contribute to early brain development.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- Nature: genes direct the basic sequence and structure of brain development (brain stem → thalamus → cerebellum → cortex) — this sequence is universal and not influenced by environment.
- Nurture: experience after birth shapes which neural connections are strengthened or pruned — e.g. language acquisition shows how stimulation develops specific pathways.
- Interaction point: genes set the initial blueprint but environment determines which parts of that blueprint are fully developed.
Mastering: Both nature and nurture clearly explained with developed examples and interaction noted.
Secure: Both explained but interaction not elaborated.
Developing: One side explained well, other only mentioned.
Emerging: Vague reference to nature and nurture without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Describe the sequence of brain development from simple neural structures in the womb through to the cortex.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should cover:
- Starting point: neural tube forms in early embryonic development.
- Brain stem develops first: controls autonomic functions (breathing, heart rate, sleep).
- Thalamus develops next: acts as a relay for sensory processing.
- Cerebellum develops: coordinates movement and balance, continues maturing into early childhood.
- Cortex develops last: responsible for higher cognition (language, reasoning, planning); continues maturing into the mid-twenties.
Mastering: All five stages described accurately and in correct order.
Secure: Four stages described correctly.
Developing: Three stages with some inaccuracy.
Emerging: One or two stages, limited accuracy.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the roles of nature and nurture in early brain development.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (AO1):
- Nature: the genetic blueprint determines the sequence (brain stem → thalamus → cerebellum → cortex) and the basic architecture of the brain. This is universal across humans.
- Nurture: experience shapes neural connections through synaptic strengthening and pruning. The cortex is particularly open to environmental influence due to its prolonged development.
- Example: language acquisition — babies can learn any language but acquire only those they are exposed to.

Evaluation (AO3):
- Strength of nature view: the consistency of developmental sequence across all humans regardless of culture or environment supports a strong genetic component.
- Limitation of nature-only view: identical twins do not always develop identically, suggesting environment plays a role even when genes are the same.
- Strength of nurture view: studies of children raised in deprived environments (e.g. limited stimulation) show reduced cortical development, showing experience matters.
- Limitation of nurture-only view: basic brain structures form even in the absence of stimulation, suggesting nature sets the foundation that nurture cannot override.
- Interactionist conclusion: most psychologists see development as an interaction; genes provide the scaffold, experience determines what is built on it.

Mastering: Accurate, detailed description of both roles with clear, elaborated evaluation including interaction.
Secure: Both described with some evaluation and elaboration.
Developing: Description present; evaluation brief or one-sided.
Emerging: Basic description, little evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which type of depression involves alternating episodes of very low mood and mania?
A) Unipolar depression
B) Seasonal affective disorder
C) Bipolar depression
D) Reactive depression
practice_questions.marks: C) Bipolar depression [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'negative schemas'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Definition states negative schemas are established patterns of negative thinking about oneself, the world and the future AND that they distort interpretation of experience — both elements clearly expressed.
Secure: Both elements present but one vague.
Developing: Mentions negative thoughts without reference to the schema framework or its distorting effect.
Emerging: Vague or incorrect definition.

practice_questions.text: Describe three symptoms used to diagnose unipolar depression.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per accurately described symptom up to 3 marks. Students may include: low mood; reduced energy levels; changes in sleep patterns (insomnia or hypersomnia); changes in appetite (eating more or less); decrease in self-confidence/sense of worthlessness.
Mastering: Three distinct symptoms named and briefly described (what the symptom involves).
Secure: Three symptoms named with minimal description.
Developing: Two symptoms described.
Emerging: One symptom named or a vague reference to 'feeling sad'.

practice_questions.text: Explain the biological theory of depression, referring to the role of neurotransmitters.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Names the neurotransmitter (serotonin), explains that low serotonin activity is linked to depression, identifies this as a nature explanation, and explains why (biological process, not experience), with development. Two developed points.
Secure: Serotonin named and linked to depression; nature explanation identified.
Developing: States that brain chemistry is involved but does not name serotonin or explain the mechanism.
Emerging: Vague reference to biology causing depression.

practice_questions.text: Describe the psychological theory of depression, including how negative schemas and attributions lead to low mood.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for: the theory is a nurture explanation (1); negative schemas are established negative thought patterns about self, world and future (1); these lead to pessimistic interpretation of experiences (1); negative attributions mean explaining failures as internal, stable and global causes (1); these patterns can develop through early experience and become self-sustaining (1).
Mastering: All five elements described with clear explanation of the mechanism.
Secure: Four elements.
Developing: Two or three.
Emerging: Vague reference to thinking being negative, without schemas or attributions.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the biological and psychological theories of depression.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate description of both theories (serotonin imbalance for biological; negative schemas and attributions for psychological); identifies these as nature vs nurture explanations; at least two elaborated evaluative points (e.g. biological is reductionist but supported by effectiveness of SSRIs; psychological is more holistic but negative schemas are hard to measure objectively), each developed with a reason.
Secure: Both theories described; two evaluative points with some development.
Developing: One theory described in detail; one evaluative point.
Emerging: One theory only or both described vaguely; evaluation is a single unsupported claim.
[AO1 ~4 marks; AO3 ~5 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is NOT a function of animal communication identified in the specification?
A) Survival
B) Reproduction
C) Planning future events
D) Territory
practice_questions.marks: C) Planning future events [1 mark] — this is a property of human communication not present in animal communication.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'waggle dance' as used in Von Frisch's bee study.
practice_questions.marks: The waggle dance is a figure-of-eight movement performed by a honeybee [1 mark] in which the angle of the straight waggle run indicates the direction of a food source relative to the sun, and the duration indicates its distance from the hive [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Describe three ways in which human communication differs from animal communication.
practice_questions.marks: Any three from: humans can plan ahead and discuss future events (animals cannot — they are tied to the present) [1 mark]; human language is productive — an unlimited number of novel sentences can be created (animals have a fixed signal repertoire) [1 mark]; human language is culturally learned (the specific language depends on the environment) whereas animal communication is largely innate and species-specific [1 mark]. Accept other relevant distinctions with development.

practice_questions.text: A researcher studies how wolves howl to communicate with each other. Using your knowledge of animal communication, explain what functions this communication is likely to serve and what it cannot do.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies two of the four limited functions (e.g. territory — howls mark pack boundaries and warn off rival packs; survival — howls can alert pack members to danger) explicitly linked to the wolf example; explains what the communication cannot do (e.g. wolves cannot discuss future events or hypothetical situations, showing the limitation of animal communication compared to human language).
Secure: One function identified and explained, and one limitation noted.
Developing: Names a function without fully explaining it, or mentions limitation vaguely.
Emerging: Vague reference to animal communication without specific functions or limitations.

practice_questions.text: Describe Von Frisch's bee study of animal communication.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate aim (how bees communicate food location/distance), method (observation of returning forager bees in the hive), results (round dance = nearby food; waggle dance = distant food with angle = direction relative to sun, duration = distance), and conclusion (bees use a coded movement system to communicate food location, though limited to food function) — all four elements.
Secure: Three elements described accurately.
Developing: Two elements or one in good detail; some inaccuracy.
Emerging: Vague account with limited specific detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the differences between human and animal communication.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate description of animal communication (four limited functions, fixed signals, tied to present context); Von Frisch's bee study as evidence; properties of human communication not in animals (planning ahead, discussing future/past, abstract topics, productivity, cultural learning); evaluation includes at least two developed points (e.g. Von Frisch shows animal communication can be sophisticated and symbolic, yet still limited; comparing them may be unfair as both serve their purpose; human language's productivity is qualitatively different).
Secure: Description of most content; evaluation covers two points with some development.
Developing: Describes some differences; evaluation underdeveloped.
Emerging: Brief description; minimal evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is the main coding used in short-term memory?
A) Semantic
B) Visual
C) Acoustic
D) Tactile
practice_questions.marks: C) Acoustic [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'short-term memory'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Precise definition stating that STM is the memory store that holds a limited amount of information (approximately 7 items) for a brief period (around 15–30 seconds), coded mainly acoustically.
Secure: Clear definition capturing limited capacity and brief duration.
Developing: Partial definition — may mention limited capacity or brief duration but not both.
Emerging: Vague attempt such as ‘memory that does not last long.’

practice_questions.text: Describe the features of the long-term memory store.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: All three features (coding = semantic, capacity = potentially unlimited, duration = potentially permanent/lifetime) described accurately with clear psychological language.
Secure: Two features described correctly with accurate terminology.
Developing: One feature described correctly; others missing or inaccurate.
Emerging: Vague response that does not use the terms coding, capacity or duration accurately.

practice_questions.text: Sasha reads a new phone number and keeps repeating it to herself until she can dial it. Use the multi-store model to explain what is happening in Sasha's memory.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies STM and rehearsal, explains that information entered STM (limited capacity, acoustic coding), and that Sasha is rehearsing to keep it active and potentially transfer it to LTM; clearly references the scenario.
Secure: Correct use of STM and rehearsal with reference to the scenario; explanation is clear.
Developing: Identifies STM or rehearsal but explanation is limited or only loosely linked to the scenario.
Emerging: Names a store without meaningful explanation or scenario engagement.

practice_questions.text: Describe the multi-store model of memory.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Describes all three stores (sensory register, STM, LTM) with coding, capacity and duration for each; explains how information flows between them via attention (sensory → STM) and rehearsal (STM → LTM); uses accurate terminology throughout.
Secure: All three stores described with most features correct; flow between stores mentioned.
Developing: Two stores described; one store or flow mechanism missing.
Emerging: Names the stores without describing their features or the flow of information.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the multi-store model of memory.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (AO1): Three stores — sensory register (large capacity, brief duration, sense-specific coding), STM (acoustic coding, ~7 items, ~15–30 seconds), LTM (semantic coding, unlimited capacity, potentially permanent). Rehearsal transfers STM to LTM; information not attended to in sensory register is lost; information not rehearsed in STM decays.
Evaluation (AO3): Strength — supported by research evidence; Murdock’s serial position curve study provides evidence for separate STM and LTM stores. Weakness — oversimplified; STM and LTM are not single unitary stores (LTM has episodic, semantic and procedural divisions). Rehearsal as the only LTM transfer route is questioned — emotionally significant events can enter LTM without deliberate rehearsal.
Mastering: Accurate, detailed description of all three stores plus at least two developed evaluation points with elaboration.
Secure: Stores described and two evaluation points made with some elaboration.
Developing: At least two stores described; one evaluation point with limited elaboration.
Emerging: Brief description; evaluation absent or only one undeveloped point.

practice_questions.text:
Which type of neuron carries information from the sense organs to the central nervous system?
A) Motor neuron
B) Relay neuron
C) Sensory neuron
D) Efferent neuron
practice_questions.marks: C) Sensory neuron [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'synapse'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise definition identifying it as the tiny gap between two neurons across which neurotransmitters (chemical messengers) pass — both elements stated [2 marks].
Secure: Correct core idea — a gap between neurons — without reference to chemical transmission [1 mark].
Developing: Vague reference to a space or connection between cells [0–1 mark].
Emerging: Incorrect or irrelevant [0 marks].

practice_questions.text: Describe the process of synaptic transmission.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per accurate step up to 3 marks. Students may include: an action potential reaches the pre-synaptic neuron; neurotransmitters are released from vesicles into the synapse; neurotransmitters bind to receptor sites on the post-synaptic neuron; this causes excitation or inhibition; neurotransmitters are broken down or taken back up via reuptake.
Mastering: Three clear sequential steps using accurate terminology.
Secure: Three steps identified but some terms imprecise.
Developing: Two steps described.
Emerging: One step or a vague description of chemicals crossing a gap.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between excitation and inhibition in synaptic transmission.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear distinction between excitation (increases likelihood of post-synaptic neuron firing) and inhibition (decreases likelihood), with an explanation of why the balance between them matters for normal brain function. Two developed points.
Secure: Both concepts correctly defined with some explanation of their effects.
Developing: One concept correctly described or both partially described.
Emerging: Vague reference to signals being “sent” or “blocked” without using correct terms.

practice_questions.text: Describe Hebb's theory of learning and neuronal growth, including the aim, the key idea and the evidence that supports it.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for: Hebb proposed the theory in 1949 (1); the theory states that repeated co-firing of two neurons strengthens the synapse between them (1); often summarised as 'neurons that fire together, wire together' (1); this means that practice and repetition physically change the brain by creating stronger neural connections (1); later research into long-term potentiation (LTP) supports this mechanism (1).
Mastering: All five points included with clear explanation of the mechanism.
Secure: Four points included.
Developing: Two or three points.
Emerging: Vague reference to learning changing the brain without specifying the mechanism.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate Hebb's theory of learning and neuronal growth.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate description of the theory (year, mechanism, 'fire together wire together'), how it explains skill-learning and memory through synaptic strengthening; two elaborated evaluation points (e.g. supported by LTP research as a strength; doesn't explain forgetting or intentional learning as a weakness), each developed with a reason.
Secure: Accurate description; two evaluation points with some development.
Developing: Partially correct description; one elaborated evaluation point or two undeveloped ones.
Emerging: Basic description; evaluation is a single unsupported claim.
[AO1 description ~4 marks; AO3 evaluation ~5 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes Gibson's direct theory of perception?
A) Perception is built from prior knowledge and past experience
B) Perception depends on cultural background and emotional state
C) The environment provides sufficient information for perception without inference
D) Perception relies on the brain constructing a model of reality from incomplete cues
practice_questions.marks: C) The environment provides sufficient information for perception without inference [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'motion parallax'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Precise definition stating that motion parallax is the apparent difference in the speed and direction of movement of objects at different distances when an observer moves — near objects appear to move quickly in the opposite direction; far objects move slowly in the same direction.
Secure: Clear definition capturing the near/far speed difference during movement.
Developing: Partial definition — mentions that near and far objects appear to move differently without precision.
Emerging: Vague attempt confusing motion parallax with another depth cue.

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by 'bottom-up processing' in Gibson's theory.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Defines bottom-up processing as perception driven by raw sensory data from the environment; explains that no prior knowledge or inference is needed; links to Gibson’s view that the optic array contains sufficient information; uses accurate terminology.
Secure: Defines bottom-up processing and contrasts it with top-down (inference-based) approaches.
Developing: Describes starting from sensory data but does not explain why Gibson argues this is sufficient.
Emerging: Vague or confuses bottom-up with top-down.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate Gibson's direct theory of perception.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (AO1): Nature account; environment provides sufficient information for direct perception; optic array contains rich information; bottom-up processing; role of motion parallax — near objects appear to move fast in opposite direction, far objects move slowly in same direction, providing depth information directly.
Evaluation (AO3): Strength — high ecological validity; developed from real-world observations; explains the speed and accuracy of everyday perception. Weakness — cannot explain visual illusions (if environment provides all information, why are we misled?). Weakness — does not account for role of experience; people with restored vision after early blindness show impaired depth perception, suggesting experience does matter. Strength — has influenced practical applications such as pilot training and road design.
Mastering: Accurate description and at least two developed evaluation points with elaboration.
Secure: Description and two evaluation points with some elaboration.
Developing: Description and one evaluation point.
Emerging: Brief description; evaluation absent or undeveloped.

practice_questions.text: Explain how motion parallax provides depth information when you are moving through the environment.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that as an observer moves, near objects appear to move quickly in the opposite direction while far objects appear to move slowly in the same direction; explains that the brain uses this difference in apparent speed to judge distance; links to Gibson’s argument that this is direct information in the optic array requiring no inference; developed explanation.
Secure: Both aspects (near moves fast, far moves slowly) explained with a link to depth perception.
Developing: One aspect described; explanation limited.
Emerging: Identifies motion parallax without explaining how it provides depth information.

practice_questions.text: Describe one strength and one weakness of Gibson's direct theory of perception.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Strength — high ecological validity because Gibson studied perception in natural, real-world environments rather than artificial laboratory conditions; explains WHY this is a strength (findings more applicable to real-life perception). Weakness — cannot explain visual illusions; if the environment provides all necessary information directly, illusions should not exist; explains WHY this is a weakness (suggests the brain does more than passively pick up environmental information). Both points developed with elaboration.
Secure: Both points made with some elaboration.
Developing: One strong point with elaboration; the other less developed.
Emerging: Names a strength or weakness without meaningful elaboration.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the process of accommodation in Piaget's theory?
A) Fitting new information into an existing schema
B) Removing an old schema that no longer works
C) Changing or creating a new schema to fit new information
D) Storing information in long-term memory
practice_questions.marks: C) Changing or creating a new schema to fit new information [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define what is meant by 'conservation' in Piaget's theory of cognitive development.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise definition capturing both (1) quantity/amount stays the same, AND (2) even when the appearance changes — e.g. 'The understanding that the quantity of something remains the same even when its appearance changes, for example the same amount of water in a different-shaped container.' [2 marks].
Secure: Core idea correct but slightly vague on the appearance-change element [1 mark].
Developing: Partial idea, missing the appearance-change element [0–1 mark].
Emerging: Incorrect or very vague [0 marks].

practice_questions.text: Describe the pre-operational stage of Piaget's theory of cognitive development.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- Age range: approximately 2 to 7 years.
- Children develop language and symbolic thought.
- Egocentrism: children see the world only from their own perspective.
- Lack of conservation: children do not understand that quantity stays the same when appearance changes.
Mastering: Age range + two characteristics with clear explanation.
Secure: Two correct features.
Developing: One feature described with some accuracy.
Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: A teacher notices that eight-year-old Amara can successfully sort objects by size and colour but struggles to solve a logic puzzle that does not involve any real objects. Using Piaget's theory, explain what stage of development Amara is likely to be in.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should:
- Identify the concrete operational stage (7–11 years).
- Explain that children at this stage can reason logically but only with real/concrete objects — not hypothetical or abstract problems.
- Apply to Amara: her ability to sort real objects reflects concrete operational logic; her difficulty with the abstract puzzle reflects the limit of this stage.
- Note that formal operational thinking (abstract reasoning) has not yet developed.
Mastering: Stage named, both features applied to the scenario with developed explanation.
Secure: Stage named with two points linked to scenario.
Developing: Stage named, one feature.
Emerging: Stage misidentified or scenario ignored.

practice_questions.text: Describe Piaget's Theory of Cognitive Development, including the role of schemas, assimilation and accommodation.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should cover:
- Schemas: mental frameworks that help us understand the world.
- Assimilation: taking in new information using an existing schema.
- Accommodation: changing or creating a schema when existing ones do not fit.
- The four stages in order: sensorimotor, pre-operational, concrete operational, formal operational.
- Each stage involves a qualitatively different way of thinking, in a fixed sequence.
Mastering: Schemas, assimilation, accommodation all correctly described, four stages named in order with characteristics.
Secure: Schemas and processes correct, at least three stages.
Developing: Two stages described; assimilation/accommodation mentioned but unclear.
Emerging: One or two elements, significant gaps.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate Piaget's Theory of Cognitive Development.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (AO1):
- Schemas, assimilation and accommodation drive development.
- Four stages: sensorimotor (0–2, object permanence); pre-operational (2–7, egocentric, lacks conservation); concrete operational (7–11, logical with real objects, gains conservation); formal operational (11+, abstract reasoning).
- Sequence is universal and fixed; cannot skip stages.

Evaluation (AO3):
- Strength: highly influential in education; led to child-centred learning, discovery learning and stage-appropriate teaching.
- Strength: systematic observations and tasks provided replicable evidence for each stage.
- Weakness: he may have underestimated children's abilities — McGarrigle and Donaldson (naughty teddy study) and Hughes (policeman doll study) showed younger children could demonstrate conservation and perspective-taking when tasks were more natural and child-friendly.
- Weakness: Piaget's clinical method involved asking children questions directly, which may have confused them and led to underestimates.
- Weakness: the theory is culturally specific — not all studies in non-Western cultures find the same stage sequences or timings.

Mastering: Accurate detailed description of all four stages, plus elaborated evaluation with at least two developed points.
Secure: Three stages described correctly with two evaluation points.
Developing: Two stages described, one evaluation point.
Emerging: Brief description, little or no evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the agentic state?
A) Acting independently and taking personal responsibility
B) Being in a crowd and losing individual identity
C) Seeing oneself as carrying out the wishes of an authority figure
D) Changing behaviour to match a peer group
practice_questions.marks: C) Seeing oneself as carrying out the wishes of an authority figure [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define 'obedience' in psychology.
practice_questions.marks: Obedience is following a direct order or instruction [1 mark] from a person perceived to be in a position of authority [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Describe how proximity affects obedience according to Milgram's Agency theory.
practice_questions.marks: Proximity refers to physical or psychological closeness to the person being harmed [1 mark]. When the victim is nearby or visible, obedience decreases because the consequences of following orders become more vivid and harder to ignore [1 mark]. When the victim is in another room or out of sight, it is easier to remain in the agentic state and continue to obey [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: A manager tells a new employee to write a misleading report. The employee knows it is wrong but follows the instruction. Using Milgram's Agency theory, explain why the employee might obey.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies and explains two relevant concepts from agency theory linked precisely to the scenario (e.g. the employee has shifted into an agentic state, seeing themselves as carrying out the manager’s wishes and passing moral responsibility upward; the manager’s authority as a supervisor is a social factor that legitimises the instruction, increasing compliance).
Secure: One concept clearly explained and linked to the scenario.
Developing: Names agency theory or the agentic state but does not link clearly to the specific scenario details.
Emerging: Vague reference to authority or following orders without psychological framing.

practice_questions.text: Describe Adorno's theory of the Authoritarian Personality as an explanation of obedience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains what the Authoritarian Personality is (high deference to authority, hostility to out-groups, rigid thinking), its origins in a strict punitive upbringing, and how it explains individual differences in obedience; accurate use of psychological terminology throughout.
Secure: Describes the main features of the personality type and links to obedience; may lack detail on origins.
Developing: Identifies the personality type and one or two features but does not develop the link to obedience or origins.
Emerging: Brief, inaccurate or very vague description.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate Milgram's Agency theory of obedience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate description of agentic and autonomous states plus the four social factors (agency, authority, culture, proximity); evaluation includes at least two developed points with elaboration (e.g. empirical support from Milgram’s variations; weakness that it cannot explain why some resist; contrast with Adorno’s dispositional account).
Secure: Description of the states and most social factors; evaluation covers two points with some development.
Developing: Description of one state and one or two social factors; evaluation present but underdeveloped.
Emerging: Brief description of obedience or authority; evaluation is a single undeveloped point.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes an independent groups design?
A) The same participants take part in all conditions
B) Participants are paired on a relevant variable before being assigned to conditions
C) Different participants take part in each condition
D) Participants are randomly assigned from the same group to different conditions, but some take part in both
practice_questions.marks: C) Different participants take part in each condition [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define what is meant by a 'natural experiment'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'An experiment in which the IV occurs naturally, rather than being manipulated by the researcher, who simply measures its effect.' — both elements present.
Secure: Core idea correct — states the IV is naturally occurring and the researcher measures it.
Developing: Mentions natural setting but misses that the IV is not manipulated by the researcher.
Emerging: Incorrect or incomplete definition.

practice_questions.text: Describe one strength and one weakness of a repeated measures design.
practice_questions.marks:
Strength: individual differences are controlled — the same participants take part in all conditions, so any differences between conditions reflect the IV rather than participant differences.
Weakness: order effects can occur — participants may perform better in the second condition due to practice, or worse due to fatigue.
Mastering: Both strength and weakness clearly described with reason.
Secure: Both identified, one described well.
Developing: One point, partially explained.
Emerging: One vague point.

practice_questions.text: A researcher wants to investigate whether people solve puzzles faster in silence or with music playing. She uses the same 20 participants in both conditions. Identify the experimental design and suggest one way to control for order effects.
practice_questions.marks:
Design: repeated measures (same participants in both conditions).
Order effects control: counterbalancing — half the participants do the silence condition first, then music; the other half do music first, then silence. This ensures any practice or fatigue effects are spread equally across both conditions rather than affecting one condition more than the other.
Mastering: Design correctly identified and counterbalancing explained with mechanism.
Secure: Design correct, counterbalancing mentioned but not fully explained.
Developing: Design correct only.
Emerging: Design incorrect or missing.

practice_questions.text: Describe the three main experimental designs used in psychological research.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should cover:
- Independent groups: different participants in each condition. Strength: no order effects. Weakness: individual differences may affect results.
- Repeated measures: same participants in all conditions. Strength: individual differences controlled. Weakness: order effects (practice, fatigue).
- Matched pairs: participants paired on a relevant variable, one per pair per condition. Strength: reduces individual differences without order effects. Weakness: time-consuming; perfect matching impossible.
Mastering: All three designs with at least one strength and one weakness each.
Secure: All three described, two with strength/weakness.
Developing: Two designs described.
Emerging: One design.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate laboratory experiments and field experiments as methods used in psychology.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (AO1):
- Laboratory experiment: conducted in a controlled setting; researcher manipulates IV and controls extraneous variables closely.
- Field experiment: conducted in a real-world setting; researcher manipulates IV but participants are in their natural environment, sometimes without knowing they are being studied.

Evaluation (AO3):
- Lab strength: high control of extraneous variables; results more clearly show effect of IV; high replicability.
- Lab weakness: low ecological validity — artificial setting means participants may behave differently from everyday life (demand characteristics).
- Field strength: higher ecological validity because behaviour occurs in natural setting; reduces demand characteristics if participants are unaware.
- Field weakness: researcher has less control over extraneous variables; ethical issues if participants have not given informed consent.
- Comparison: choice between lab and field depends on whether internal validity (control) or ecological validity (real-world applicability) is more important for the research question.

Mastering: Both methods described accurately with elaborated evaluation including comparison.
Secure: Both described, evaluation present.
Developing: One method described well, one point of evaluation.
Emerging: One method, little evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes postural echo?
A) Using eye contact to signal the end of your speaking turn
B) Keeping a comfortable distance from another person
C) Unconsciously mirroring another person's body posture
D) Crossing your arms to signal disagreement
practice_questions.marks: C) Unconsciously mirroring another person's body posture [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define 'personal space' in the context of non-verbal communication.
practice_questions.marks: Personal space is the invisible zone or boundary around a person [1 mark] that they consider their own, and within which they feel comfortable or uncomfortable depending on who enters it [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Describe one piece of evidence that suggests non-verbal communication is innate.
practice_questions.marks: Research with neonates (newborn babies) provides evidence that NVC is innate [1 mark]. Neonates display basic facial expressions such as disgust and distress from birth, before they have had any opportunity to learn these through observation or imitation [1 mark]. The early appearance of these expressions suggests they are biologically programmed rather than culturally acquired [1 mark]. [OR: sensory-deprived individuals show the same emotional expressions as sighted people, supporting an innate basis — accept either example fully developed.]

practice_questions.text: A person at a party stands with arms crossed, avoiding eye contact, and stays as far from others as possible. Using your knowledge of non-verbal communication, explain what their behaviour might be communicating.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two NVC concepts precisely identified and linked to the scenario (e.g. closed posture — crossed arms signal defensiveness or discomfort, indicating unwillingness to engage; avoidance of eye contact signals lack of interest or discomfort in social interaction; maximising personal space suggests a desire to limit close social contact).
Secure: One NVC concept clearly explained and linked to the behaviour described.
Developing: Names a relevant NVC concept but does not explain how it applies to the specific behaviour in the scenario.
Emerging: Vague statements about body language or shyness without psychological framing.

practice_questions.text: Describe Yuki's study of emoticons as evidence about non-verbal communication.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate aim (to investigate cross-cultural differences in reading emotional expressions from faces), method (Japanese and American participants rated emoticons for emotional expression), results (Japanese focused on eyes; Americans focused on mouth; different emoticon conventions in each culture), and conclusion (reading NVC is at least partly culturally learned, not purely innate) — all four elements.
Secure: Three elements described accurately.
Developing: Two elements or one in good detail; some inaccuracy.
Emerging: Vague account with limited specific detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the debate over whether non-verbal communication is innate or learned.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate description of Darwin's evolutionary theory (evolved and adaptive); innate evidence (neonates, sensory-deprived); learned evidence (Yuki — cross-cultural differences in reading faces); evaluation includes at least two developed points (e.g. neonate research controlled for learning, supporting innate basis; Yuki shows cultural variation, supporting nurture; modern consensus is interaction of both; limitation of Yuki — emoticons are artificial stimuli).
Secure: Both sides of the debate described; evaluation covers two points with some development.
Developing: One side of the debate described; evaluation underdeveloped.
Emerging: Brief description of one position; minimal evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes interobserver reliability?
A) When the same researcher gets the same results on two separate occasions
B) When two or more independent observers record the same behaviours consistently
C) When a questionnaire is completed twice by the same participant
D) When experimental results can be replicated in a different laboratory
practice_questions.marks: B) When two or more independent observers record the same behaviours consistently [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define what is meant by 'qualitative data'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'Data expressed in words or descriptions rather than numbers, providing rich detail about experiences, feelings or opinions.' — both elements present and clearly linked.
Secure: Correct core idea — data in words and reference to detail or experience.
Developing: Mentions 'words' but without contrasting with numerical or quantitative data.
Emerging: Incorrect or incomplete definition.

practice_questions.text: Describe one strength and one weakness of using a questionnaire in psychological research.
practice_questions.marks:
Strength: large numbers of participants can be reached quickly and cheaply; no interviewer bias if completed independently.
Weakness: social desirability bias — participants may not answer honestly, giving responses they believe are expected rather than true answers.
Mastering: Both clearly described with developed reason.
Secure: Both identified, one developed.
Developing: One point explained.
Emerging: One vague point.

practice_questions.text: A researcher finds a positive correlation between the number of hours students spend on social media and their reported levels of anxiety. Explain what this correlation tells us and what it does not tell us.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should:
- State that a positive correlation means as social media use increases, anxiety also tends to increase (the two variables move in the same direction).
- Explain that the correlation does not tell us that social media use causes anxiety.
- Explain the third variable problem: a third variable (e.g. pre-existing stress, personality) may cause both increased social media use and increased anxiety.
- Conclude: only a controlled experiment can establish causation.
Mastering: Direction of correlation, causation limitation, third variable explanation all clear.
Secure: Causation limitation stated, third variable mentioned.
Developing: Causation limitation stated without development.
Emerging: Describes what a correlation is without addressing causation.

practice_questions.text: Describe the key features of an observation study, including the use of categories of behaviour and interobserver reliability.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should cover:
- Definition: the researcher watches and records behaviour without manipulating variables.
- Can be naturalistic (natural setting) or structured (controlled setting).
- Categories of behaviour: predetermined, clearly defined behaviours to record — makes data objective and consistent.
- Interobserver reliability: two or more observers independently record the same behaviour; their records are compared — high agreement indicates categories are clear and consistently applicable.
- Strength: ecological validity (naturalistic). Weakness: observer bias; Hawthorne effect if participants know they are being watched.
Mastering: All five elements described accurately.
Secure: Four elements present.
Developing: Two or three elements.
Emerging: General description only.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate two non-experimental research methods used in psychology.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (AO1) — any two of interviews, questionnaires, case studies, observation:
- Interview: researcher asks questions; can be structured or unstructured; produces quantitative or qualitative data.
- Questionnaire: written questions; closed (quantitative) or open (qualitative) questions; can reach large samples.
- Case study: in-depth study of single individual; uses multiple methods; rich qualitative data.
- Observation: researcher watches behaviour using predetermined categories; interobserver reliability checked.

Evaluation (AO3) of chosen two methods:
- Interview: strength = depth of data. Weakness = interviewer bias, time-consuming.
- Questionnaire: strength = large samples, cheap. Weakness = social desirability bias, low response rate may bias sample.
- Case study: strength = rich detail, unique cases. Weakness = cannot generalise, subjective.
- Observation: strength = ecological validity (naturalistic). Weakness = observer bias, Hawthorne effect.

Mastering: Two methods described accurately, with two elaborated evaluation points each.
Secure: Two methods described, evaluation for each.
Developing: Two methods described, limited evaluation.
Emerging: One method described.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a social factor that reduces bystander intervention?
A) Expertise of the bystander
B) Similarity to the victim
C) Presence of other bystanders
D) Personality of the bystander
practice_questions.marks: C) Presence of other bystanders [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define 'diffusion of responsibility' as it applies to bystander behaviour.
practice_questions.marks: Diffusion of responsibility is the reduction in an individual's sense of personal obligation to help [1 mark] that occurs when other bystanders are present, as each person assumes someone else will act [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Describe one way in which the cost of helping affects bystander intervention.
practice_questions.marks: High costs of helping reduce the chance of intervention [1 mark]. For example, if helping involves personal danger, significant effort or embarrassment, a bystander is less likely to act [1 mark]. Low-cost actions such as alerting emergency services are more likely to be taken because the effort and risk are small [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: A woman collapses on a busy high street. Many people are watching but nobody helps. Using your knowledge of bystander behaviour, explain why bystanders might not intervene.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two factors clearly identified and explained with explicit links to the scenario (e.g. the large number of bystanders creates diffusion of responsibility — each person on the busy street assumes someone else will help; people look to others for cues and if nobody reacts, the situation seems less urgent).
Secure: One factor clearly explained and linked to the scenario.
Developing: Names a relevant factor but does not clearly connect it to the scenario.
Emerging: Vague statement about crowds or people not helping without psychological framing.

practice_questions.text: Describe Piliavin's subway study of bystander behaviour.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate aim (effect of victim characteristics on bystander behaviour in a naturalistic setting), method (field experiment on New York subway, confederate collapsed as ill or drunk victim, observation of helping), results (ill victim helped faster and more often; help typically from same-race bystander; passengers left rather than help over time), and conclusion (cost-benefit calculation and similarity affect bystander decisions) — all four elements present and precise.
Secure: Three of the four elements described accurately.
Developing: Two elements or one element in good detail; some inaccuracy.
Emerging: Vague account with limited specific detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the social and dispositional factors that affect bystander intervention.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate description of social factors (presence of others/diffusion of responsibility, cost of helping) and dispositional factors (similarity, expertise); evaluation includes at least two developed points with elaboration (e.g. Piliavin supports the role of cost and similarity; ethical issues with the study; limitation that situational explanations underestimate individual differences in empathy).
Secure: Description of most factors; evaluation covers two points with some development.
Developing: Description of two or three factors; evaluation present but limited.
Emerging: Brief, underdeveloped description; minimal evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which lobe of the brain is primarily responsible for processing visual information?
A) Frontal lobe
B) Parietal lobe
C) Temporal lobe
D) Occipital lobe
practice_questions.marks: D) Occipital lobe [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'localisation of function'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise definition stating that specific areas of the brain are responsible for specific functions, with a supporting example such as the motor cortex controlling movement or the occipital lobe processing vision [2 marks].
Secure: Core principle correct — different brain areas have different functions — without a supporting example [1 mark].
Developing: Vague reference to different brain areas doing different things [0–1 mark].
Emerging: Incorrect or irrelevant [0 marks].

practice_questions.text: Describe the function of the cerebellum.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per accurate point up to 3 marks. Students may include: located at the back and base of the brain; coordinates smooth and precise movement; involved in balance and motor coordination; involved in procedural learning/acquiring motor skills through practice; without it movements become clumsy and uncoordinated.
