Mastering: Location, core function and one additional specific role all stated clearly.
Secure: Location and function stated.
Developing: Function stated without location or vice versa.
Emerging: Vague description only.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Penfield's study provides evidence for localisation of function in the brain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Describes the method (electrical stimulation of awake patients during surgery), identifies what was found (motor cortex stimulation → movements; temporal lobe stimulation → vivid memories), and explains how this supports localisation (different areas produced different, predictable responses). Two developed, linked points.
Secure: Describes method and links one result to the principle of localisation.
Developing: Describes the study but does not explicitly link results to localisation.
Emerging: Vague reference to Penfield studying the brain without accurate content.

practice_questions.text: Describe Penfield's study of the interpretive cortex, including the aim, method, results and conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each for: aim (to map cortex functions in epilepsy patients during surgery); method (electrical probe applied to the cortex; patients kept awake; responses recorded); results (motor cortex stimulation produced movements; temporal lobe stimulation triggered memories); conclusion (functions are localised to specific cortical areas); naming the temporal lobe region Penfield called the 'interpretive cortex'.
Mastering: All five elements included.
Secure: Four elements.
Developing: Two or three elements.
Emerging: Vague description without accurate AMRC structure.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the localisation of function in the brain, including reference to Penfield's study.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate description of the lobes and their functions (at least three); description of Penfield's study (aim, method, results, conclusion); two elaborated evaluation points (e.g. supported by multiple sources of evidence — strength; complex behaviours involve networks, not single areas — weakness; brain plasticity as a challenge to strict localisation), each developed with reasoning.
Secure: Description of at least two lobes and Penfield's findings; two evaluation points with some development.
Developing: Partial description; one evaluation point.
Emerging: Basic mention of brain areas without functions; evaluation is a single unsupported claim.
[AO1 ~4 marks; AO3 ~5 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the correct conclusion from McGarrigle and Donaldson's naughty teddy study?
A) Pre-operational children never understand conservation
B) Children showed better conservation ability when the change was accidental
C) The naughty teddy confused children and made them perform worse
D) Conservation is fully developed by age 4
practice_questions.marks: B) Children showed better conservation ability when the change was accidental [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define what is meant by 'egocentrism' in Piaget's theory.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise definition capturing (1) the inability to take another's viewpoint/perspective, AND (2) linked to the pre-operational stage or the idea that the child assumes others see/think the same as them — e.g. 'The inability of a child in the pre-operational stage to appreciate that others have a different viewpoint from their own.' [2 marks].
Secure: Core idea correct but one element missing or vague [1 mark].
Developing: Partial — confuses egocentrism with selfishness only [0–1 mark].
Emerging: Incorrect [0 marks].

practice_questions.text: Describe how Piaget's theory can be applied to education.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- Teaching should be matched to the child's developmental stage.
- Hands-on and practical learning suits the concrete operational stage (7–11).
- Abstract or hypothetical teaching is only appropriate from the formal operational stage (11+).
- Discovery learning: children should be allowed to explore and construct understanding themselves.
Mastering: Three clear applications linked to specific stages.
Secure: Two applications, one stage referenced.
Developing: General point about matching teaching to age.
Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain one strength and one weakness of McGarrigle and Donaldson's naughty teddy study.
practice_questions.marks:
Strength: The task was more naturalistic and child-friendly than Piaget's standard conservation task, making it more ecologically valid — children could respond naturally rather than second-guessing an adult's deliberate action.
Weakness: The naughty teddy condition may have distracted children with the 'naughty teddy' narrative, accidentally cueing the correct answer rather than testing pure cognitive ability — this reduces validity.
Mastering: Both strength and weakness developed with explanation of why.
Secure: Both identified, one developed.
Developing: One point, partially explained.
Emerging: One brief point.

practice_questions.text: Describe Hughes' policeman doll study.
practice_questions.marks:
Aim: To investigate whether pre-operational children could take another person's perspective when the task was more meaningful.
Method: A model divided by walls was used; two toy policemen were placed at positions within it. Children were asked to hide a boy doll so neither policeman could see it, requiring the child to take the visual perspective of both policemen.
Results: Most children successfully hid the doll in a position hidden from both policemen, demonstrating perspective-taking ability.
Conclusion: Pre-operational children are less egocentric than Piaget claimed; when tasks are meaningful and involve an understandable scenario, even young children can take another's perspective.
Mastering: All four elements accurate and clearly stated.
Secure: Aim, results and conclusion present; method slightly vague.
Developing: Two elements; results or conclusion missing.
Emerging: Gist only.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the challenge to Piaget's findings from McGarrigle and Donaldson's naughty teddy study and Hughes' policeman doll study.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (AO1):
- Piaget claimed pre-operational children lacked conservation and were egocentric.
- McGarrigle and Donaldson: naughty teddy scattered counters accidentally; more children conserved correctly than in Piaget's standard task.
- Hughes: children hid doll from two policemen correctly, demonstrating perspective-taking.
- Both suggest children are cognitively more capable earlier than Piaget claimed.

Evaluation (AO3):
- Strength of both studies: more ecologically valid — tasks were naturalistic and meaningful to children.
- Limitation: both used small or specific samples; may not generalise to all children.
- Counter to McGarrigle and Donaldson: the teddy narrative may have cued children, so results could reflect the fun of the game rather than true conservation ability.
- Counter to Hughes: the task was more complex (two policemen), which could mean children guessed correctly without true perspective-taking.
- Overall evaluation: Piaget's findings may have been task-dependent rather than stage-dependent; the challenges suggest stage boundaries are more flexible than Piaget believed.

Mastering: Both studies described accurately with elaborated evaluation.
Secure: Both described, two evaluation points.
Developing: One study described well, one evaluation point.
Emerging: One study described, no evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly explains the recency effect?
A) Items at the start of a list are recalled because they were rehearsed into LTM
B) Items in the middle of a list are recalled because they are distinctive
C) Items at the end of a list are recalled because they are still active in STM
D) Items at the start of a list are recalled because they are still active in STM
practice_questions.marks: C) Items at the end of a list are recalled because they are still active in STM [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'primacy effect'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Precise definition stating that the primacy effect is the tendency to recall items at the beginning of a list better than those in the middle, because early items receive more rehearsal and are transferred to long-term memory.
Secure: Clear definition capturing ‘beginning of a list’ and ‘better recall’ with a link to rehearsal or LTM.
Developing: Identifies better recall for items at the start but does not explain why.
Emerging: Vague or confused with recency effect.

practice_questions.text: Describe what a serial position curve looks like and what it shows.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Describes the U-shaped curve with recall probability on the vertical axis and serial position on the horizontal; names both the primacy effect (high recall at start) and recency effect (high recall at end) with lower recall in the middle; explains what the shape shows about memory.
Secure: Describes the U-shape and names both effects.
Developing: Describes the shape or names one effect; the other is missing.
Emerging: Vague description without naming the effects or shape.

practice_questions.text: Describe Murdock's serial position curve study.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Covers aim (to investigate serial position effect in free recall), method (participants heard word lists at a set rate, recalled in any order immediately after), results (U-shaped curve, primacy and recency effects, middle items recalled least), and conclusion (supports separate STM and LTM stores); precise psychological language used throughout.
Secure: All four elements present; one may lack full development.
Developing: Three elements present; one missing or inaccurate.
Emerging: Only finding or only aim mentioned; structure of study not evident.

practice_questions.text: Explain what would happen to the recency effect if participants were asked to count backwards for 30 seconds before recalling the word list. Use your knowledge of the multi-store model in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States that the recency effect would disappear; explains that the distracting task prevents rehearsal and causes STM traces to fade; links to the multi-store model (STM has short duration without rehearsal); the primacy effect would remain because those items are already in LTM.
Secure: Correctly predicts disappearance of recency effect with clear reference to STM duration; primacy effect mentioned.
Developing: Predicts the recency effect changes but explanation of why is limited or does not clearly reference the multi-store model.
Emerging: Recognises a change but cannot explain it in terms of the model.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate Murdock's serial position curve study.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (AO1): Aim to investigate the serial position effect; participants heard word lists and recalled freely; results showed a U-shaped curve with better recall for early (primacy) and late (recency) items than middle items; conclusion supports separate STM and LTM stores.
Evaluation (AO3): Strength — controlled laboratory study allows replication; extraneous variables controlled. Weakness — low ecological validity because memorising unrelated word lists is unlike everyday memory. Strength — results replicated consistently across many studies, supporting reliability. Weakness — limited to one type of memory task; may not reflect memory for meaningful material.
Mastering: Accurate full study description plus two or more developed evaluation points with elaboration.
Secure: Study described and two evaluation points made with some elaboration.
Developing: Study described with at least one evaluation point.
Emerging: Brief or inaccurate description; evaluation absent or undeveloped.

practice_questions.text:
Which explanation of visual illusions applies to Rubin's vase?
A) Fiction
B) Misinterpreted depth cues
C) Ambiguity
D) Size constancy
practice_questions.marks: C) Ambiguity [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'top-down processing'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Precise definition stating that top-down processing is perception influenced by prior knowledge, expectations and context, which are applied from higher cognitive processes to interpret incoming sensory data.
Secure: Clear definition capturing the role of prior knowledge in interpreting sensory data.
Developing: Partial definition — mentions knowledge or experience without explaining how they apply to perception.
Emerging: Confuses top-down with bottom-up processing.

practice_questions.text: Describe the Kanizsa triangle illusion and explain why it occurs according to Gregory.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Describes the Kanizsa triangle as three pac-man shapes that produce the perception of a white triangle in the centre even though no triangle is drawn; explains it as a fiction illusion where the brain constructs a contour that does not exist because this is the most plausible interpretation; uses accurate terminology.
Secure: Describes the illusion and names fiction as the explanation.
Developing: Describes the illusion without explaining the category of illusion.
Emerging: Vague description or incorrect explanation.

practice_questions.text: The Müller-Lyer illusion shows two lines of equal length, but one appears longer because of arrow fins at each end. Use Gregory's constructivist theory to explain why this illusion occurs.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies misinterpreted depth cues and size constancy; explains that the arrow fins resemble corners of buildings (inward fins = inside corner, further away; outward fins = outside corner, nearer); size constancy makes the ‘further’ line appear longer; links directly to the scenario; uses accurate terminology.
Secure: Correct identification with clear scenario engagement.
Developing: Names a relevant concept but explanation is limited.
Emerging: Names Gregory without meaningful explanation.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate Gregory's constructivist theory of perception.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (AO1): Nurture account; brain constructs perception using sensory input plus prior knowledge and expectations; top-down processing; when inferences go wrong, visual illusions result. Four explanations: ambiguity (Rubin’s vase, Necker cube), misinterpreted depth cues (Ponzo, Müller-Lyer), fiction (Kanizsa triangle), size constancy (Ames Room). Role of prior experience in building perceptual hypotheses.
Evaluation (AO3): Strength — explains visual illusions; Gibson’s theory cannot. Strength — supported by studies showing perception is affected by context, culture and expectation. Weakness — cannot easily explain why everyday perception is so accurate if it relies on potentially error-prone inferences. Weakness — the role of prior knowledge is difficult to isolate and measure scientifically.
Mastering: Accurate description and two or more developed evaluation points with elaboration.
Secure: Description and two evaluation points with some elaboration.
Developing: Description and one evaluation point.
Emerging: Brief description; evaluation absent or undeveloped.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the Ponzo illusion is explained by Gregory's constructivist theory.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Describes the Ponzo illusion (two equal horizontal lines between converging lines; upper appears longer); identifies misinterpreted depth cues as the explanation category; explains that the converging lines trigger linear perspective, making the upper line appear further away; size constancy then makes the upper line appear larger; all linked to the constructivist principle that the brain uses prior knowledge of depth to construct perception.
Secure: Illusion described, depth cue misinterpretation and size constancy both mentioned.
Developing: Illusion described; one mechanism (cue or size constancy) explained but not both.
Emerging: Names the illusion without meaningful explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes how SSRIs work to treat depression?
A) They increase the production of new neurons in the hippocampus
B) They block serotonin reuptake, increasing its availability at the synapse
C) They suppress the activity of the sympathetic nervous system
D) They stimulate the production of dopamine in the frontal lobe
practice_questions.marks: B) They block serotonin reuptake, increasing its availability at the synapse [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT)'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Definition states CBT is a talking therapy AND that it helps people identify and change negative thought patterns and the behaviours that maintain depression — both elements clearly expressed.
Secure: Both elements present but one vague.
Developing: Mentions talking or changing thoughts but without both elements of the full definition.
Emerging: Vague or incorrect definition.

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between a reductionist and a holistic approach to treating depression.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks. Students should: define reductionist as explaining/treating depression through a single, simpler mechanism (biology/brain chemistry) (1); define holistic as treating the whole person including thoughts, behaviour and social context (1); apply these terms to antidepressants (reductionist) and CBT (holistic) (1).
Mastering: Both terms defined and correctly applied to a specific treatment each.
Secure: Both terms defined, one applied.
Developing: One term defined with application.
Emerging: Vague description of the difference without using the correct terms.

practice_questions.text: Explain how CBT helps to improve mental health in people with depression.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies the core mechanism (challenges negative automatic thoughts); explains the cognitive element (restructuring thought patterns) and behavioural element (reintroducing avoided activities); explains why this improves mood (thinking and behaviour change creates a positive cycle). Two developed points.
Secure: Identifies negative thought patterns as the target and explains at least one technique.
Developing: States that CBT helps people think differently but without explaining the mechanism.
Emerging: Vague reference to talking helping or thinking being changed.

practice_questions.text: Describe Wiles' study of the effectiveness of CBT, including the aim, method, results and conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each for: aim (to investigate whether CBT added to antidepressants improved outcomes for treatment-resistant patients); method (two conditions — medication as usual vs medication plus CBT; symptoms measured over time); results (CBT group showed significantly greater improvement than medication-only group); conclusion (CBT effective even when medication alone has not worked); implication (supports a combined/holistic treatment approach).
Mastering: All five elements.
Secure: Four elements.
Developing: Two or three.
Emerging: Vague reference to CBT working without AMRC structure.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the use of antidepressants and CBT as treatments for depression.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate description of both treatments (how SSRIs work, what CBT does); identifies reductionist/holistic perspectives; uses Wiles' study as evidence for CBT; two elaborated evaluative points (e.g. antidepressants don't address thought patterns — depression may return; CBT teaches lasting skills but is resource-intensive), each developed with reasoning.
Secure: Both treatments described; two evaluative points with some development.
Developing: One treatment described in detail; one evaluative point.
Emerging: Vague description of both; evaluation is a single unsupported claim.
[AO1 ~4 marks; AO3 ~5 marks]

practice_questions.text:
In Bruner and Minturn's study, what was the independent variable?
A) Whether participants were hungry or not
B) Whether participants had first seen a series of letters or a series of numbers
C) Whether the ambiguous figure looked more like a letter or a number to each participant
D) The level of brightness of each image shown to participants
practice_questions.marks: B) Whether participants had first seen a series of letters or a series of numbers [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'perceptual set'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Precise definition stating that perceptual set is a readiness to perceive things in a particular way, influenced by factors such as expectation, motivation, emotion and culture.
Secure: Clear definition capturing the readiness/predisposition aspect and at least one shaping factor.
Developing: Partial definition — describes perceiving what you expect without defining set precisely.
Emerging: Vague attempt such as ‘when you expect to see something.’

practice_questions.text: Describe how culture can affect perception.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that people from different cultural environments develop different perceptual sets; describes the carpentered environment concept (cultures with rectangular buildings are more susceptible to certain illusions); explains the mechanism (brain uses repeatedly seen patterns as default interpretive frameworks); uses accurate terminology.
Secure: Describes cultural variation in perception with a relevant example and some mechanism explanation.
Developing: States that culture affects perception without developing the mechanism or giving a specific example.
Emerging: Vague statement that people in different places see things differently.

practice_questions.text: Describe Gilchrist and Nesberg's study of motivation and perception.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Aim (to investigate whether motivation affects perception), method (participants with varying food/water deprivation shown images of food and drink, asked to adjust brightness to match what they saw), results (hungrier/thirstier participants set brightness higher than less deprived participants), conclusion (motivation/physiological need affects perception, making need-relevant stimuli appear more vivid) — all four elements present, precise language throughout.
Secure: All four elements present; one may lack full development.
Developing: Three elements present; one missing or inaccurate.
Emerging: Only findings mentioned; study structure not evident.

practice_questions.text: Omar is a football fan. He is watching a match and believes the referee has made a mistake in calling his team offside. Omar insists the player was onside. Use the concept of perceptual set to explain his perception.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies perceptual set; links to expectation and/or motivation; explains that Omar’s support for his team creates a motivational set predisposing him to perceive the decision in favour of his team, and his expectation that his team should succeed shapes his interpretation of the ambiguous position; links directly to the scenario; uses accurate terminology.
Secure: Correct identification of perceptual set with scenario engagement.
Developing: Names perceptual set or motivation/expectation but limited scenario engagement.
Emerging: General reference to bias without using perceptual set terminology.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate two factors that affect perception.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (AO1): Any two of — culture (carpentered environments affect illusion susceptibility), motivation (Gilchrist and Nesberg: deprivation makes need-relevant stimuli appear brighter), emotion (anxious individuals perceive ambiguous stimuli as threatening), expectation (Bruner and Minturn: prior context determines perception of ambiguous figure). For each: describe the factor and the relevant study evidence.
Evaluation (AO3): Strength — both named studies used controlled experimental methods with clear IV and DV, giving high internal validity. Weakness — artificial stimuli limit ecological validity. Weakness — individual differences (culture, personality) mean findings may not generalise to all. Strength — research supports Gregory’s constructivist theory, linking perceptual set evidence to top-down processing.
Mastering: Two factors described with study evidence and two developed evaluation points.
Secure: Two factors described and two evaluation points with some elaboration.
Developing: Two factors described; one evaluation point.
Emerging: One factor described; evaluation absent or undeveloped.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a growth mindset according to Dweck?
A) The belief that intelligence is a fixed trait you are born with
B) The belief that ability can be developed through effort and learning from mistakes
C) The preference for visual over verbal learning
D) High self-confidence regardless of past performance
practice_questions.marks: B) The belief that ability can be developed through effort and learning from mistakes [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define what is meant by 'self-efficacy'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise definition capturing (1) belief in one's own ability/capacity to succeed, AND (2) linked to a specific task or situation — e.g. 'A person's belief in their own ability to succeed at a specific task or challenge.' [2 marks].
Secure: Core idea correct but 'specific task' element missing or vague [1 mark].
Developing: Vague reference to confidence; not clearly about task-specific belief [0–1 mark].
Emerging: Incorrect [0 marks].

practice_questions.text: Describe Dweck's Mindset Theory of learning.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- There are two mindsets: fixed and growth.
- Fixed mindset: believes ability is unchangeable; avoids challenge; gives up at failure.
- Growth mindset: believes ability can be developed through effort; embraces challenges; learns from failure.
- Type of praise received can influence which mindset develops (ability praise → fixed; effort praise → growth).
Mastering: Both mindsets defined with a point about praise or self-efficacy.
Secure: Both mindsets described without praise/self-efficacy.
Developing: One mindset described.
Emerging: Vague reference to fixed/growth.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the type of praise a child receives can influence the development of a fixed or growth mindset.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should:
- Explain that ability-based praise ('You're so clever') promotes fixed mindset: signals intelligence is a fixed trait, making children avoid challenges where they might fail.
- Explain that effort-based praise ('You worked really hard') promotes growth mindset: signals that effort leads to success, making children more willing to take on challenges.
- Explain the mechanism: children internalise messages about what determines success (talent or effort) and adjust their behaviour accordingly.
Mastering: Both types of praise explained with the mechanism linking praise to mindset and behaviour.
Secure: Both types explained, mechanism partially described.
Developing: One type of praise and its effect.
Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Describe Willingham's Learning Theory and his criticism of learning styles.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should cover:
- Willingham is a cognitive scientist who criticised learning styles theory.
- His argument: preference for a style does not mean learning is better in that style.
- The content should determine the format (spatial content → visual; verbal content → words), not the student's preference.
- The 'meshing hypothesis' (matching teaching to preferred style improves outcomes) is not consistently supported by experimental evidence.
- His theory suggests teachers should use the format that best fits the content, not student preferences.
Mastering: Preference vs effectiveness distinction clear, content-drives-format principle, reference to lack of evidence.
Secure: Three elements present.
Developing: Two elements.
Emerging: One element.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate Dweck's Mindset Theory of learning.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (AO1):
- Two mindsets: fixed (ability is unchangeable) and growth (ability can be developed through effort).
- Fixed mindset: avoids challenges, gives up, threatened by failure.
- Growth mindset: embraces challenges, persists, learns from failure.
- Role of praise: ability praise reinforces fixed mindset; effort praise promotes growth mindset.
- Self-efficacy: growth mindset supports belief in capacity to succeed.

Evaluation (AO3):
- Strength: has practical application — growth mindset interventions in schools have been widely used and some studies show positive effects on attainment and resilience.
- Strength: supported by research evidence from Dweck's own controlled studies linking mindset to academic outcomes.
- Weakness: some replication studies have found smaller effects than Dweck's original research, raising questions about how reliably school interventions work.
- Weakness: the theory may oversimplify — mindset exists on a spectrum, not a binary, and may vary by subject or context.
- Weakness: not all researchers agree that simple praise manipulation produces lasting mindset change.

Mastering: Accurate description of both mindsets and role of praise, with elaborated evaluation of at least two points.
Secure: Both mindsets described, two evaluation points present.
Developing: One mindset described well, one evaluation point.
Emerging: Brief description, little evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which scanning technique detects changes in blood oxygen levels to produce real-time images of brain activity?
A) CT scan
B) PET scan
C) fMRI scan
D) EEG
practice_questions.marks: C) fMRI scan [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'cognitive neuroscience'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise definition stating it is the study of how brain structure and/or function relates to cognitive processes such as memory, perception or behaviour — both elements present [2 marks].
Secure: Links the brain to mental processes but does not specify what type of brain information (structure/function) or the type of mental process [1 mark].
Developing: Vague reference to how the brain relates to thinking [0–1 mark].
Emerging: Incorrect or irrelevant [0 marks].

practice_questions.text: Describe how a PET scan works.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per accurate point up to 3 marks. Students may include: the patient is injected with a radioactive substance (often glucose); the most active brain areas use the most glucose and emit the most radioactivity; the scanner detects these emissions and creates a colour-coded map of brain activity.
Mastering: All three steps described in sequence, using accurate terms.
Secure: Two steps described.
Developing: States the scan shows activity but without explaining the mechanism.
Emerging: Vague mention of detecting the brain without any mechanism.

practice_questions.text: Explain how evidence from neurological damage, such as a stroke, supports the principle of localisation of function.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Defines stroke (blocked blood supply kills neurons in that region), identifies that effects depend on which region is damaged, provides a specific example (e.g. motor cortex damage → paralysis; Broca's area damage → speech production affected), and explicitly links this to localisation. Two developed, linked points.
Secure: Defines stroke and links damage in a specific area to a specific function loss.
Developing: States stroke damages the brain and causes problems, but without linking to specific areas and their functions.
Emerging: Vague reference to brain damage affecting behaviour.

practice_questions.text: Describe Tulving's 'gold' memory study, including the aim, method, results and conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each for: aim (to investigate whether episodic and semantic memory are supported by different brain areas); method (PET scanning while participants recalled episodic or semantic memories); results (episodic memory → right prefrontal cortex; semantic memory → left prefrontal cortex); conclusion (the two memory types are neurologically distinct/lateralised); significance (provides evidence for both different memory systems and localisation of function).
Mastering: All five points accurately described.
Secure: Four points.
Developing: Two or three.
Emerging: Vague reference to Tulving studying memory with a scan, no AMRC structure.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the use of brain scanning techniques to investigate brain function.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate descriptions of all three techniques (CT, PET, fMRI) with the key difference between structural (CT) and functional (PET/fMRI) scans; reference to Tulving's study as an example of PET use; two elaborated evaluative points (e.g. objective, non-invasive evidence from living participants — strength; correlation not causation, artificial setting — weaknesses), each developed with a reason.
Secure: Two techniques described accurately; two evaluative points with some development.
Developing: One or two techniques described; one evaluative point.
Emerging: Mentions scanning without accurate description; evaluation is a single unsupported statement.
[AO1 ~4 marks; AO3 ~5 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes 'standardised procedures' in psychological research?
A) Using the same participants across all conditions
B) Ensuring every participant experiences the same conditions and instructions
C) Using a random sample from the target population
D) Comparing results to a standardised population norm
practice_questions.marks: B) Ensuring every participant experiences the same conditions and instructions [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define what is meant by 'validity' in psychological research.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'The extent to which a study measures what it claims to measure and whether findings can be applied beyond the study context.' — both elements present.
Secure: Core idea correct — measures what it claims to measure and some reference to generalisability.
Developing: Confuses reliability and validity, or mentions only one aspect without the other.
Emerging: Incorrect or incomplete definition.

practice_questions.text: Describe how counterbalancing is used to reduce order effects in a repeated measures design.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- In a repeated measures design, the same participants complete all conditions, creating a risk of order effects (practice or fatigue).
- Counterbalancing: half the participants complete condition A then B; the other half complete B then A.
- This spreads any order effect equally across both conditions so it does not bias one condition more than the other.
Mastering: What it is, how it is done, and why it works — all clear.
Secure: Two of three elements.
Developing: Mentions counterbalancing and order effects without explaining the mechanism.
Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: A researcher studying stress tells participants the study is about 'reaction times'. After the study, she explains its true purpose and gives participants the chance to withdraw their data. Identify two ethical issues shown in this scenario and explain how each was dealt with.
practice_questions.marks:
Issue 1: Deception — participants were not told the true purpose (told it was about reaction times). Dealt with: debrief after the study disclosed the real purpose.
Issue 2: Right to withdraw data — participants were given the opportunity to withdraw their data after the study ended.
(Credit also: protection from harm if stress is discussed; informed consent was partly compromised by deception.)
Mastering: Two issues identified and dealt with, both linked to the scenario.
Secure: Two issues, one linked to scenario.
Developing: One issue identified and dealt with.
Emerging: One issue named only.

practice_questions.text: Describe the ethical guidelines set out by the British Psychological Society for research with human participants.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should cover at least four of:
- Informed consent: participants must be told what the study involves and agree freely.
- Right to withdraw: participants can leave at any time without penalty.
- Confidentiality: personal data kept private; participants cannot be identified from published results.
- Protection from harm: no lasting physical or psychological damage.
- Debrief: full explanation of the study's purpose after completion; option to withdraw data.
- Deception: only used when unavoidable; must be addressed in debrief.
Mastering: Four or more issues described with how each is addressed.
Secure: Three issues described with solutions.
Developing: Two issues named and dealt with.
Emerging: Two issues named without solutions.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the importance of standardised procedures, randomisation and counterbalancing in planning psychological research.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (AO1):
- Standardised procedures: fixed instructions and conditions for all participants; ensures consistency; enables replication.
- Randomisation: chance allocation of participants to conditions; reduces systematic bias; controls individual differences between groups.
- Counterbalancing: in repeated measures designs, AB order for half, BA for the other half; reduces order effects (practice, fatigue).
- All three increase reliability and/or validity of the study.

Evaluation (AO3):
- Strength of standardisation: increases reliability — same procedure can be replicated to check results.
- Limitation: over-standardised procedures may reduce ecological validity if conditions become too artificial.
- Strength of randomisation: controls individual differences between groups, improving internal validity.
- Limitation: random allocation does not guarantee equal groups, especially with small samples.
- Strength of counterbalancing: effectively reduces order effects without requiring a separate group.
- Limitation: even with counterbalancing, some tasks are impossible to counterbalance (e.g. if order exposure permanently changes behaviour).

Mastering: All three described accurately with elaborated evaluations.
Secure: All three described, two evaluations.
Developing: Two topics described, one evaluation.
Emerging: One topic, little evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a criterion used to diagnose addiction according to the ICD?
A) Experiencing hallucinations when using a substance
B) A higher priority given to the substance than to other activities or obligations
C) Using a substance to enhance physical performance
D) Feeling anxious without the substance for the first time
practice_questions.marks: B) A higher priority given to the substance than to other activities or obligations [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'aversion therapy'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Definition states aversion therapy pairs the substance with an unpleasant stimulus AND that this creates a conditioned negative response that deters further use — both elements clearly expressed.
Secure: Both elements present but one vague.
Developing: Mentions making the substance unpleasant but without the conditioning mechanism.
Emerging: Vague or incorrect definition.

practice_questions.text: Describe two differences between addiction and substance misuse.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks. Students may include: addiction involves loss of control and compulsive use; misuse involves harmful use without necessarily being dependent (1); addiction involves withdrawal symptoms or strong cravings; misuse may not (1); addiction means the substance takes priority over other obligations; misuse need not reach this level (1).
Mastering: Two clearly distinct differences, each developed.
Secure: Two differences identified, one developed.
Developing: One difference described.
Emerging: Vague distinction between the two terms.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Kaij's twin study supports the biological theory of addiction.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States what Kaij studied (twins with history of alcohol abuse); states that MZ twins showed higher concordance than DZ twins; explains why this supports a genetic explanation (MZ share 100% DNA, DZ ~50%, so higher MZ concordance = genetic contribution); explicitly labels this as a nature explanation. Two developed, linked points.
Secure: States the finding (MZ higher concordance) and links to genetics.
Developing: States Kaij studied twins and found a genetic link but without explaining the logic of the twin method.
Emerging: Vague reference to genetics causing addiction without using Kaij's findings.

practice_questions.text: Describe the psychological theory of addiction, including the role of peer influence.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for: this is a nurture explanation (1); peer influence means friends/social group normalise substance use (1); social learning — observing peers rewarded for use increases imitation (1); if substance use is accepted in the group, conformity pressure is strong (1); this explains why addiction clusters in social groups and why young people are particularly vulnerable to peer pressure around substances (1).
Mastering: All five elements with clear explanation of the mechanism.
Secure: Four elements.
Developing: Two or three.
Emerging: Vague reference to friends causing addiction.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the therapies used to treat addiction, including reference to reductionist and holistic perspectives.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate descriptions of aversion therapy (mechanism, reductionist) and self-management programmes/12-step (mechanism, holistic); applies these terms explicitly; two elaborated evaluative points (e.g. aversion therapy quick but doesn't address underlying causes — relapse risk; 12-step is holistic and sustained but requires personal commitment), each developed.
Secure: Both therapies described; two evaluative points with some development.
Developing: One therapy described in detail; one evaluative point.
Emerging: Vague description; evaluation is a single unsupported claim.
[AO1 ~4 marks; AO3 ~5 marks]

before.exam_tip_html: For Kaij’s study, the key finding to state is that MZ twins had a higher concordance rate than DZ twins, and explain why this supports a genetic explanation (MZ share 100% DNA; DZ share ~50%). Examiners want you to use the term “concordance rate” and explain what the comparison between twin types tells us. On the 9-mark question, apply “reductionist” and “holistic” explicitly when evaluating the therapies — these terms directly earn marks.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes deindividuation?
A) Working harder when observed by others in a crowd
B) Feeling greater personal responsibility in a large group
C) Losing individual identity and sense of personal accountability in a crowd
D) Deliberately choosing to help others in an anonymous setting
practice_questions.marks: C) Losing individual identity and sense of personal accountability in a crowd [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define 'social loafing' as it applies to collective behaviour.
practice_questions.marks: Social loafing is the tendency for individuals to put in less effort when part of a group [1 mark] because they assume that others will make up for their reduced contribution [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Describe how deindividuation can lead to antisocial behaviour in crowds.
practice_questions.marks: Deindividuation occurs when people lose their individual identity within a crowd [1 mark]. This reduces personal accountability — because individuals feel anonymous, the self-monitoring and moral constraints that usually govern behaviour weaken [1 mark]. As a result, people are more likely to follow the crowd’s prevailing antisocial norms, such as joining in aggression or vandalism [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: At a music festival, some concert-goers behave antisocially, vandalising stalls. Others in the same crowd are helpful and look after strangers. Using your knowledge of collective behaviour, explain why people in the same crowd might behave so differently.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two factors precisely identified and linked to the scenario (e.g. deindividuation — the large crowd and anonymity of the festival reduce personal accountability, allowing antisocial behaviour; morality — individuals with strong personal values of fairness resist the crowd’s antisocial norms and act helpfully instead).
Secure: One factor clearly explained and linked to the scenario.
Developing: Names a relevant concept but does not connect it clearly to the scenario.
Emerging: Vague reference to crowd influence without psychological framing.

practice_questions.text: Describe the social factors that affect collective behaviour in crowds.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate, detailed description of all three social factors (social loafing, deindividuation, culture) with psychological terminology; clear explanation of how each factor operates in a crowd context; coherent organisation.
Secure: Describes two or three social factors with reasonable accuracy and some development.
Developing: Describes one or two factors with limited development.
Emerging: Brief, vague or inaccurate description of one factor.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the social and dispositional factors that affect crowd and collective behaviour.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate description of social factors (social loafing, deindividuation, culture) and dispositional factors (personality, morality); evaluation covers at least two developed points (e.g. deindividuation explains both prosocial and antisocial outcomes; but social factors alone cannot account for individual variation within a crowd — dispositional factors are also needed; social loafing effect is not universal).
Secure: Description of most factors; evaluation covers two points with some development.
Developing: Describes a few factors; evaluation present but underdeveloped.
Emerging: Brief description; minimal evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes 'effort after meaning'?
A) Trying hard to recall every detail of an event
B) Distorting information to fit existing knowledge and make it seem logical
C) Using a memory cue to trigger recall of a forgotten item
D) Repeating information to transfer it from STM to LTM
practice_questions.marks: B) Distorting information to fit existing knowledge and make it seem logical [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'false memory'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Precise definition stating that a false memory is a recollection of an event that did not actually occur, or a significantly distorted memory of one that did, arising from reconstructive processes or post-event suggestion.
Secure: Clear definition capturing the idea of remembering something inaccurate or imagined.
Developing: Partial definition — may say ‘imagining something happened’ without linking to memory processes.
Emerging: Vague attempt such as ‘a wrong memory.’

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by a schema and explain how schemas can distort memory.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Defines schema as a mental framework of knowledge built from past experience; explains that during recall, schemas fill in gaps with expected information rather than actual details; links to effort after meaning or Bartlett’s theory; uses accurate terminology.
Secure: Defines schema and gives a developed explanation of how it causes distortion.
Developing: Defines schema or explains distortion, but not both clearly.
Emerging: Vague reference to knowledge or memory without linking the two.

practice_questions.text: Describe Bartlett's War of the Ghosts study.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Aim (investigate how memory for unfamiliar story changes over time), method (British participants read and recalled a Native American folk tale over varying intervals), results (participants shortened, rationalised and changed the story to fit familiar cultural schemas; unfamiliar details omitted or replaced), conclusion (memory is active reconstruction shaped by prior knowledge) — all four elements present, precise language used.
Secure: All four elements present; one may lack full development.
Developing: Three elements present; one missing or inaccurate.
Emerging: Only the results or a vague gist of the study; structure not evident.

practice_questions.text: Jaya witnessed a car accident and later told police what she saw. A week later, her account had changed: she remembered a red car being involved, even though there was no red car. Use Bartlett's Theory of Reconstructive Memory to explain why Jaya's memory changed.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies reconstructive memory and schemas; explains that Jaya’s recall was shaped by her prior knowledge and expectations (schemas) about what accidents look like; effort after meaning led her to fill in gaps with plausible details; links directly to the scenario (adding a red car).
Secure: Correct identification of reconstructive memory with clear scenario engagement.
Developing: Names reconstructive memory or schemas but explanation limited or only loosely linked to Jaya’s account.
Emerging: Identifies that memory can be wrong without using Bartlett’s framework.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate Bartlett's Theory of Reconstructive Memory.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (AO1): Memory is active reconstruction shaped by schemas and effort after meaning; we fill in gaps to make memories coherent; supported by War of the Ghosts study — participants altered and shortened an unfamiliar story over time. Three factors affecting accuracy: interference, context, false memories.
Evaluation (AO3): Strength — ecological validity; using a story is closer to real-world memory than word lists. Strength — practical applications; understanding of reconstructive memory has influenced eyewitness testimony research and police interview techniques. Weakness — lack of controlled methodology; Bartlett did not use standardised procedures or statistical analysis. Weakness — theory does not explain all types of memory error; some highly accurate ‘flashbulb’ memories suggest memory is not always distorted.
Mastering: Accurate, detailed description and at least two developed evaluation points with elaboration.
Secure: Description and two evaluation points with some elaboration.
Developing: Description and one evaluation point.
Emerging: Brief description; evaluation absent or undeveloped.

practice_questions.text:
A researcher collects data on the number of hours students sleep per night. The results for eight students are: 6, 7, 8, 7, 5, 9, 7, 7. What is the mode of this dataset?
A) 6
B) 7
C) 7.5
D) 8
practice_questions.marks: B) 7 [1 mark — the mode is the most frequently occurring value; 7 appears four times]

practice_questions.text: Define what is meant by 'primary data'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'Data collected first-hand by the researcher themselves, specifically for their own study.' — both elements present.
Secure: Core idea correct — mentions researcher collecting data directly for their own purpose.
Developing: Mentions researcher collecting data but omits 'first-hand' or 'for own study'.
Emerging: Confuses primary data with quantitative data or secondary data.

practice_questions.text: A psychology student records the following scores on a memory test: 12, 15, 10, 14, 11, 13, 12. Calculate the mean and range for this dataset.
practice_questions.marks:
Mean: (12 + 15 + 10 + 14 + 11 + 13 + 12) = 87; 87 ÷ 7 = 12.43 (allow 12.4 or 12).
Range: 15 − 10 = 5.
Mastering: Both calculations correct with working shown.
Secure: Both answers correct, no working shown.
Developing: One calculation correct.
Emerging: Correct attempt at method but calculation error(s).

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a bar chart and a histogram, and state when each would be used in psychological research.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should:
- Bar chart: used for discrete or categorical data; bars have gaps between them to show that the categories are separate (e.g. counts of participants by eye colour, or mean scores per condition).
- Histogram: used for continuous data grouped into ranges; bars touch each other because the underlying data is continuous (e.g. distribution of ages, scores in intervals).
- Distinction: the presence or absence of gaps reflects whether data is discrete (bar chart) or continuous (histogram).
Mastering: Both types defined with correct data type, distinction clear, example for each.
Secure: Both types defined and distinguished.
Developing: One type defined correctly, other partially.
Emerging: Vague or confused.

practice_questions.text: Describe the key features of a normal distribution and explain its importance in psychological research.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should cover:
- Shape: symmetrical, bell-shaped curve.
- Mean, median and mode all have the same value at the centre of the distribution.
- Most scores cluster around the mean; fewer scores appear at the extremes.
- Example: intelligence test scores or height in a large population.
- Importance: provides a reference for interpreting scores (typical vs unusual); many psychological variables approximate it; assumed by many statistical tests.
Mastering: All five elements present and accurate.
Secure: Four elements present.
Developing: Shape and mean/median/mode equality described.
Emerging: Basic description only.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the use of the mean and median as measures of central tendency in psychological research.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (AO1):
- Mean: add all values, divide by n. Uses all the data. Affected by outliers.
- Median: middle value when data ordered. Not affected by outliers. Best used when extreme values present.
- Mode: most frequent value — not discussed as the focus is mean and median.
- When to use: mean when data is symmetrically distributed with no extreme outliers; median when data is skewed or outliers present.

Evaluation (AO3):
- Strength of mean: uses all data values, giving the most sensitive representation of the dataset; works well for normally distributed data.
- Weakness of mean: distorted by outliers — a single extreme score can give a misleading picture of typical performance.
- Example: if nine participants score 10 and one scores 100, the mean is 19 — not representative of most scores.
- Strength of median: resistant to outliers; gives a better picture of the typical score when data is skewed.
- Weakness of median: ignores the actual values of scores, only using position — loses information.
- Comparison: choice depends on the data; for normally distributed data use mean; for skewed or outlier-affected data use median.

Mastering: Both measures accurately described, strengths and weaknesses of each elaborated, comparison made.
Secure: Both described, two evaluation points.
Developing: Both described, one evaluation point.
Emerging: One measure described.
